In Kill, that deity (representing the gods), for example, begins by puffing on his cigarette, while below him a small boy (representing the people) scribbles furiously.

But like pretty much everything she does, it is a remarkable work, so maybe let’s just agree that as a starting point and move on. As the title suggests, it comprises four pieces. The first three are short, the last (‘Imp’) is fairly long.
Caryl Churchill is a national treasure and her new work, four plays GLASS.KILL.BLUEBEARD.IMP playing at The Royal Court, are a reminder of that.

Seemingly with no other interlink that the same actors, each play is different from one another, with a different concept, it Is a true triumph and evidence of a brilliant playwright that she can make such interesting plays, which last for not long at all.
Direction by James MacDonald (assisted by Grace Gummer) is expert, bringing Churchill’s words to blazing, haunting life.

Maybe in comparison to the older casts that follow, this younger set of performers never really get into their stride. Despite being suspended ethereally on a wooden plank in the air the piece feels rather flat. Kill is up next, following the blood-soaked stories of the curse of the house of Atreus.
Intriguing and amusing, referencing classical drama, and provoking questions about many things, it also provides impeccable acting.
For the more passive audience member, it’s an unusual, creative spectacle.

cn.t: Churchill's quartet of short plays pack a powerful punch with politically-charged surrealism and dark humor, showcasing the legendary playwright's inimitable voice and creative range across wildly different tales of murder, mischief, and the absurd.
